Culture · Noh · Tokyo

The star is not the whole stage.

At the National Noh Theatre today, young performers are exposing an easily missed truth about one of the world’s oldest living theatres: the masked protagonist cannot create its world alone.

By Yuji Shimizu · YUJI @ Japan
October 20, 2026 · 07:10 JST · 6 min read

At 1 p.m. in Sendagaya, the polished cypress stage of Tokyo’s National Noh Theatre will hold a public examination disguised as a performance. The 41st Seishokai is a showcase for trainees and younger professionals. Its program includes four maibayashi—dance-and-music excerpts without full costumes and masks—and the Kyogen comedy Fune Funa. Tickets cost ¥1,300, a modest price for a close look at how a tradition survives.

The immediate surprise is who the training is designed to protect. International introductions to Noh often begin with the shite, the principal actor who may wear a mask and embody a god, warrior, woman, ghost or demon. The National Theatre’s six-year training system instead concentrates on three other specialties: waki supporting actors, hayashi instrumentalists and Kyogen actors. Japan calls them the noh-gaku sanyaku, the “three roles” of Noh.

700roughly seven centuries of continuous Noh tradition
6 yearsbasic and specialist national training
41stSeishokai training showcase today

A protagonist needs someone to ask the question

Many Noh stories begin with a traveler arriving at a famous place. That figure is often the waki: a priest, official or warrior who belongs to the living world. The mysterious person he meets may later be revealed as the ghostly shite. The waki’s questions invite the story into existence. He may spend long stretches seated at the side, but still controls what the audience is able to learn.

The music is just as specialized. The hayashi ensemble may combine the nohkan flute with shoulder, hip and stick drums. The drummers’ audible calls are not spontaneous cheering. They mark time, coordinate musicians and shape the silence around a movement. A first-time listener can hear what sounds like irregular cries and beats; a trained performer hears a system of cues precise enough to support dance that has been transmitted through schools for generations.

The hidden mechanism is specialization: Noh endures not because one actor memorizes an old play, but because separate lineages learn how to meet on the same stage.

Kyogen adds another shift in tone. It has its own comic repertoire built around dialogue and physical action, and Kyogen actors also appear inside Noh as ai figures who explain background between sections. Today’s Fune Funa turns on language itself: two characters dispute how to pronounce the word for boat. That makes a supposedly ancient form feel unexpectedly familiar. A tiny disagreement about usage becomes performance.

Four dances, four schools, one afternoon

The program identifies the performers and schools rather than presenting “Noh” as one uniform style. Ryoji Taguchi performs Takasago in the Kanze school; Yuichi Kanoh performs Hashitomi in the Kita school; Misa Hayashi performs Kumasaka in the Konparu school; and Ryoichi Takeda performs Kakitsubata in the Hosho school. The Kyogen item features Yusuke Oku of the Izumi school.

Those titles span very different imaginative worlds. Takasago is associated with paired pines, harmony and longevity. Hashitomi draws on the world of The Tale of Genji and the memory of Yugao. Kumasaka revisits a defeated bandit as a restless spirit, while Kakitsubata transforms irises and classical poetry into the identity of a woman. A stripped-down maibayashi does not stage each drama in full. It reveals the skeleton: chant, instrumental pattern and dance.

The schools matter because transmission is not merely a national script copied identically. Performers inherit role-specific vocabularies, musical patterns and interpretive choices. The National Theatre began its three-role training in 1984, the year after the venue opened, because relying only on private apprenticeship would leave vulnerable specialties with too few successors. Its course combines three years of basic work with three years of specialist training.

What an overseas visitor should watch

Do not wait for realistic scenery. The permanent roofed stage, bridgeway and painted pine are the visual world; a few steps may represent a long journey. Watch where a performer looks, how a fan changes meaning, and how stillness makes one turn of the body feel large. Listen for the space between a drum call and a footfall. Noh does not hide its musicians at the bottom of a pit: the people constructing time remain visible.

Today’s event is not a tourist demonstration and not a claim that trainees are already masters. It is a professional development performance, one stage in a long process. That distinction is the reason to notice it. Heritage survives through rehearsal, evaluation and opportunities to perform before an audience—not through age alone.

For language learners, the program also shows why Japanese vocabulary changes what the eye can see. Learn shite, waki, hayashi and kyogen, and a single “Noh actor” becomes a network of different jobs. DraMap’s promise is to learn Japanese while playing; a live stage offers the same broader lesson. A word is not only a translation. Sometimes it reveals the structure that was there all along.
